_doc: TEMPORAL BUDGET — every temporal call of the repository, DECLARED with its motive (2026-08-20). SINGLE SOURCE, consumed by `test/temporal-budget-gate.test.js`. DETECTION is NOT here: it lives in `rules/temporal-call.yml` (ast-grep). Strict separation — the rule detects without exemption, this file plus its test carry the POLICY and the ratchet.
_doc_name: Named `temporal`, never `budget` alone: in this repository `budget.js` already means the EMISSION budget (characters per frame). Two different quantities must never share a word.
_doc_why: LOCAL, THE KERNEL KNOWS: a process exit, a closed socket, an `EADDRINUSE` are FACTS the OS delivers. Waiting a fixed number of milliseconds instead of asking the authority that KNOWS is not caution, it is a BUG that fires on a loaded machine. A delay is admissible only when no authority can be asked.
_doc_motives: Exactly TWO motives are admissible and the test refuses any other word: `distant` = no authority is reachable (a third-party host, a network peer: nobody local can answer) and `undecidable` = alive-versus-frozen, i.e. the halting problem (nothing can tell whether the awaited event will ever happen).
_doc_ratchet: The declared `count` must EQUAL the measured one. Higher means the ratchet is stale, so LOWER IT (a declaration nobody uses widens the budget for free, in silence — same doctrine as a stale layer justification). Lower means a new temporal call appeared: prove its motive, or remove the call. A file absent from `budget` is held at ZERO.
_doc_blind_cell: DECLARED, not hidden: a temporal call written INSIDE a template literal (the source of a child script — real case, `test/session-store.test.js` line 95, an `Atomics.wait`) is invisible to the AST, because for the parser it is a STRING and not a call. That is the correct verdict about THIS file (the call belongs to another program, which is not in this perimeter) and it is also a way out that nobody may take deliberately. No cheap mechanical fix exists: parsing every string as a program would turn every code sample in every comment into a defect.

motives.distant: No authority is reachable — whatever knows lives on another machine and may never answer.
motives.undecidable: Alive-versus-frozen: nothing local can decide whether the awaited event will ever occur (halting problem).

src/deadline.js.why: The anti-zombie deadline. The harness does NOT always send EOF on stdin (Claude Code Windows bug anthropics/claude-code#68626), so the hook waits for an `end` event that may never come, and no local authority can say whether it will. The timer BOUNDS that infinity, it optimises nothing. Threshold 30 s, measured under load — see `deadline.md`.

src/judge-runner.js.why: The bound of ONE adopter judge run (option `wrapUp`, 2026-10-04). A judge is ANY command (a script, a suite of judges, a call to a model): whether one that has not answered yet is slow or will never answer is the halting problem, and no local authority can tell. Every other end of a run is a kernel FACT (`exit`, `close`, `error`), never a delay. When it fires, the whole process tree is killed and the verdict is given at once (an orphan may hold the pipes for ever, so waiting for `close` would hang the hook). Ceiling 540 s, below the 600 s the wiring declares on the Stop hook.

src/lock.js.why: TWO occurrences, and they are different animals. ① The sleeping back-off (Atomics.wait) between two attempts at the cross-process lock: the holder is another PROCESS, and whether it is running, frozen or already gone cannot be settled from here. Chosen SLEEPING rather than a tight loop, because burning a core would slow down the very holder we wait for; what BOUNDS it is the lock's own fail-open timeout. ② The clock comparison `UNIDENTIFIED_HOLDER_MS` — visible to this budget only since 2026-08-23, when the clock atoms were added to the rule. It judges ONE case: a lock directory whose holder pid was never recorded, because the process died between the atomic `mkdirSync` and the syscall that writes the record. There is literally nobody to ask — the kernel cannot answer about a pid nothing wrote down — so it is `undecidable` in the strict sense. 🛑 It is NOT the old STALE_MS: an IDENTIFIED holder is decided by the KERNEL (`process.kill(pid, 0)`, ESRCH = a proof of death), never by this number. Widening it back to identified locks re-opens the silent lost update that TLC exhibits as `StateStaleForcing`.

test/judge-runner.test.js.why: The tree-kill cell asks the KERNEL again whether a killed grandchild is gone (`kill(pid, 0)`, plus its `/proc` state on Linux, where a killed process lingers as a zombie until reaped). Whether another process has been reaped YET is not decidable from the test process; the wait between two asks is bounded (100 × 50 ms) and its exhaustion fails the cell, never passes it. MEASURED 2026-10-04 on the ubuntu CI runner: a few microseconds of ticks (the first version) read a reaped-later zombie as alive.

test/deadline.test.js.why: Watchdog that SIGKILLs the spawned hook. This suite exists precisely to prove the hook dies when stdin never ends: what is awaited is, by construction, possibly infinite. Without this timer a red test would hang the runner for ever.

test/serve-stall-concurrency.test.js.why: The cell must produce a SLOW CLIENT — a request whose headers arrive and whose body does not, which is the exact shape the `serve-stall` instrument exists to record. The delay IS the thing under test, never a wait for something knowable: no authority can be asked 'when should this client be late', because lateness is the fixture. ⚠️ DECLARED LATE, 2026-09-18: the file shipped the night before and the gate could not see it, a tracked-file perimeter being blind to what git does not yet know — the net catches it one run after the commit, by design.

test/http-listeners.test.js.why: Two yields between two OBSERVATIONS of a FORKED daemon: has it reached its listening state, and is a given socket of its set really open. What nothing local can decide is WHEN the child will get there, or whether it ever will. Every loop is BOUNDED and its exhaustion is a reported verdict, never a silent pass. 🔴 SECOND CALL, 2026-09-20, AND IT CORRECTS THIS VERY ENTRY: the sentence that stood here — "a connect to a port nobody holds is refused at once" — was MEASURED FALSE. The accept queue is capped per socket (232 on this platform) and Microsoft documents that a FULL queue answers WSAECONNREFUSED, the same code a closed port answers. On a saturated machine ONE attempt therefore cannot tell "nobody opened this socket" from "the machine had no millisecond to spare", and a full-suite run produced exactly that: [true,false,true,true] on four sockets a healthy daemon had opened. The retry makes load cost TIME and never a verdict, and it strengthens BOTH directions — a port that must be silent must now refuse every attempt for the whole bound, where a squatting daemon would answer one of them. ⚠️ The connect bound on the socket itself is of the same family: on Windows a SYN to a loopback address is never retransmitted (SIO_TCP_INITIAL_RTO, uv__is_loopback), so an attempt that loses one hangs for the OS default instead of answering. It turns a hang into an ANSWER and decides nothing.

test/dual-transport.test.js.why: Cell 4 forks a shell against a rendezvous a LIVE occupant already holds, and asserts the shell dies. On macOS CI (2026-08-31) it neither bound nor died: the cell timed out at 30 s with an empty stderr, and a timeout cannot tell apart a bind never attempted, an errno other than EADDRINUSE sent down the degradation path, and a probe that never settled. Whether that child will EVER exit is not decidable from here — it is the halting question, on a kernel nobody on this side owns. The bound does not retry and does not widen anything: the cell still FAILS, it fails while NAMING what the child wrote and that it was still alive.

test/http-daemon-lifecycle.test.js.why: Waits for the KERNEL to have OBSERVED an event (a watch being armed, a peer socket seen as closed) before asserting on the daemon's reaction. The kernel holds the fact but exposes no signal for 'you have now observed it', so 'has it noticed yet?' is not decidable from the test process. Any NEW wait added to this suite must first prove that no observable exists (an event, an exit code, a bound port): these five are a ceiling, not a licence. The fifth bounds cell 7's wait for a filesystem notification: macOS CI (2026-09-01) delivered NONE at all for a write to an existing file inside a watched directory, where Linux delivers one, and Node documents that behaviour as platform-defined. Whether an event that has not arrived ever will is the halting question, asked of a kernel this side does not own. The bound retries nothing and widens nothing: it turns a 30 s timeout blaming a regression that does not exist into a NAMED refusal to decide.

test/stale-code-guard.test.js.why: ONE yield (`settle`) between two observations of a FOREIGN process: has the daemon written its journal line yet, has it bound its port yet. The fact belongs to another process and no signal says 'you may now observe it', so 'has it got there yet?' is not decidable from this one. Nothing here concludes from time passing: every loop asks the kernel again and gives up the moment the child is gone. The yield exists so a poll does not saturate a core while the kernel does the work. — SECOND CALL (2026-08-31), cell 6bis: it waits for a metadata-only KERNEL NOTIFICATION to end a paranoid daemon started with serve:false. With no request the point-of-use comparison never runs, so that notification is the ONLY thing that can end it, and whether a given filesystem will ever deliver one is not decidable from here: MEASURED on all three CI runners, none did, and the cell timed out at 60 s on a healthy repository. The bound turns that infinity into a NAMED non-decision (ctx.skip UNMEASURED) instead of a red reporting a regression that does not exist. 🛑 It is not a widened limit: waiting longer cannot make an absent notification arrive. — THIRD CALL (2026-09-20), cell ②: the SAME bound, for the SAME reason, on the cell that proves the healthy direction of what 6bis proves by sabotage. It waits for a metadata-only KERNEL NOTIFICATION to appear in the journal as `code-unchanged`, and whether a given filesystem will ever deliver one is not decidable from here — 6bis was bounded on 2026-08-31 after all three CI runners delivered none, and this one was left unbounded, so it timed out at 60 s and reported a regression that does not exist. 🔑 THE DEFECT WAS THE ASYMMETRY, never the number of seconds: two cells testing one fact cannot have two regimes. 🛑 The decidable half — the daemon stayed ALIVE and SERVING after the touch, which IS the 2026-08-24 outage — is asserted BEFORE the bound and unconditionally, so the named non-decision costs the journal line and never the proof.

test/vendor-deadline.test.js.why: The same watchdog as `deadline.test.js`, applied to the vendored copy shipped to the hook fleet: a hook under test may legitimately never exit, which is the very defect being measured.

test/doctor.test.js.why: Cases 14a/14c hide settings.json, spawn the doctor and put the file back, and "put it back" must happen AFTER the child has actually met the absence or the cells measure nothing. That used to be a literal 400 ms and it RACED node's own startup: MEASURED 2026-09-19, the read landed after the restore, so 14a was vacuously green and its negative check 14c reported it by failing. The synchronisation is now an OBSERVATION of the child (the doctor announces its wait on stdout) and the remaining call is the CEILING on that observation: if the sentence never comes, the wait must end and let the assertions speak instead of hanging until the suite timeout and reporting a regression that did not happen. Whether a line that has not arrived ever will is the halting question, and nothing local can answer it — the value only needs to be LARGE, never right.

tools/doctor.js.why: TWO occurrences of `createEventWaiter`, and they are different animals. ① The `setTimeout` fallback tick, paired with a real `fs.watch` on settings.json's parent directory as the PRIMARY signal. `readSettingsThrough` (src/doctor-wiring-pure.js) retries on ENOENT because WHATEVER OTHER PROCESS transiently holds/renames the file during a loaded SessionStart may or may not release it soon — nobody local can say when, or whether, which is the halting question this budget names `undecidable`. HISTORY: a FIRST fix (2026-09-14) used a fixed '20 x 250ms' delay sized to ONE measured 3828ms stall on ONE machine; the operator correctly rejected it as the same bug with a bigger number (a slower/busier machine could need far more). This SECOND fix reacts to the real kernel signal instead of guessing a duration; the setTimeout is only a low-cost periodic double-check for the documented case where fs.watch misses an event (nodejs.org/api/fs, and the existence of `chokidar` as the cross-platform reference for exactly this problem), spaced by exponential backoff with full jitter (industry-standard retry spacing, AWS/Google Cloud SDK guidance) rather than a fixed interval. ② The clock comparison `giveUp = () => Date.now() - debut >= plafondMs` — the safety CEILING itself. It never estimates how long a stall 'normally' lasts (that was the exact defect of the first fix); it only decides when to eventually stop waiting for an event that may never come, which is undecidable in the strict sense — nothing local can tell whether the file will EVER become readable. Its value (2 minutes) is legitimate precisely BECAUSE it does not need to be 'right', only large enough to never fire on a healthy machine.

test/invocation-snapshot-restart.test.js.why: The cell yields between two OBSERVATIONS of a daemon it does not own: it asks the KERNEL whether the port answers, and only a successful connection or a refusal decides — nothing is ever concluded from the time that passed. Whether a child that has not yet bound ever will is the halting question, so the loop is a NON-DECISION bounded so a red cell fails instead of hanging the runner for ever. The two facts this suite actually reads are both delivered by the OS: the exit CODE of the child (90, its own stale-code verdict) and the presence of the snapshot it wrote on the way out. Removing the yield would busy-spin a core for no verdict.

test/daemon-idle-exit.test.js.why: ONE call site (`pause`) that yields between two OBSERVATIONS of a daemon this suite forks and does not own: while it starts (the kernel answers each connect), between requests that must keep an on-demand daemon alive, and across three windows a `login` daemon must survive. Nothing is concluded from the time that passed — the verdicts are the child's exit CODE, the kernel's answer to a request and the daemon's own journal. Whether a process that has not left ever will is the halting question, so the waits are bounded by the cell, never by a guessed duration of the daemon's work.

src/hooks/http-server.js.why: TWO occurrences, and they are different animals. ② (2026-09-29) THE IDLE WINDOW of an on-demand daemon (`http.lifecycle`): ONE `setTimeout` call site re-armed from itself, closing on EQUALITY of the shared activity counter and never on a clock comparison. What it waits for is whether ANOTHER harness session will ever ask — the future of a human, which no local authority can answer. A request that arrives moves the counter and the next window simply re-arms; the timer is never armed in `login` mode. ① ONE bounded wait, on the STOP path only (`drainOwner`). With a pool the state owner is a worker thread, and `process.exit` kills a worker outright — no event, no `finally` — so the daemon asks it to save and waits for the flag that says it HAS. Without that wait, the most frequent death of this process (the stale-code exit, dozens of times a day by design) would kill the owner mid-save and lose the arrival order of every invocation in flight, while looking exactly as clean as it always did. Whether a thread that has not answered ever will is the halting question, asked of an isolate this side cannot inspect. The wait RE-CHECKS and its exhaustion costs exactly what the old behaviour cost: nothing is retried, nothing is guessed, the process simply leaves. 🛑 With NO pool there is no owner and this line is never reached — the historical path is untouched.

src/hooks/owner-client.js.why: THE round trip to the state owner. It must BLOCK: `pretool-core` asks `pendingFor` inside `withLock`, and `lock.js` busy-waits, so an asynchronous answer there would let one thread hold the lock while another spins for the whole deadline. The bound is not a delay and buys no speed — measured, one round trip costs 1.48-1.65 microseconds against ~1,300 for one acquisition of the cross-process lock this daemon already pays. It exists because a BARE `Atomics.wait` blocks FOR EVER on a single missed wake-up: the value changed before the sleeper looked, so the notify it waits for has already happened. That exact shape hung a probe for ten minutes on 0.4 s of CPU on 2026-09-19. Bounded AND re-checking, or the idiom is wrong; the ceiling only has to be LARGE, never right, and its exhaustion is a NAMED refusal saying the owner is dead or wedged — never a longer wait, and never a local answer, which would be the second memory this whole design removes.

src/hooks/state-owner-thread.js.why: The owner SLEEPS between rounds instead of spinning: burning a core would slow down the very threads it answers. It reads the doorbell BEFORE scanning, so a request posted between the scan and the wait has already changed the expected value and the wait returns at once — the classic lost wake-up, closed by ordering rather than by a timer. The bound is belt and braces on top of that ordering, and it is cheap: the slice only ever costs anything when a notify was MISSED, which is precisely the case nothing local can decide. Whether a wake-up that has not arrived ever will is the halting question.

test/thread-pool-differential.test.js.why: One yield between two OBSERVATIONS of a FORKED daemon reaching its listening state, exactly as `http-listeners.test.js` declares. The kernel answers each attempt immediately and exactly (a connect to a port nobody holds is refused at once, and no delay is ever used as a verdict); what nothing local can decide is WHEN the child will get there, or whether it ever will. The loop is BOUNDED and its exhaustion is a reported FAILURE carrying the child stderr, never a silent pass — a cell that gave up quietly would read exactly like a daemon that never bound, which is the defect this suite exists to catch.

_doc_witnesses: ANTI-INERT, the guarantee that holds everything else. Every `pattern:` atom of `rules/temporal-call.yml` MUST be paired here with a line of code whose detection is REQUIRED (written to the OS tmpdir, scanned, detection asserted). An atom without a witness is REFUSED, so an atom added tomorrow stays RED until someone proves it sees anything at all. The tmpdir and not `state/`: `ast-grep` HONOURS `.gitignore`, and witnesses written into an ignored folder are invisible — measured in this repository on 2026-08-06.

witnesses.setTimeout($$$): const t = setTimeout(() => { child.kill('SIGKILL'); resolve({ dead: false }); }, 30000);

_doc_witness_origin: `setTimeout` and `Atomics.wait` are copied from the REAL occurrences of this repository (`vendor-deadline.test.js`, `lock.js`). The other five atoms have ZERO occurrence here and are PREVENTIVE: their witnesses are the canonical forms of the escape hatches they close (`timers/promises`, a homemade `sleep`). Said plainly rather than passed off as encountered forms.
_doc_floors: ANTI-VACUITY — a gate that analyses nothing goes green, this repository's worst defect class. The perimeter is DERIVED from `git ls-files` (151 JavaScript files measured on 2026-08-20) and held above a floor, and the total number of temporal calls found is held above a floor too. Both floors sit deliberately far below the measurement: they catch a BLIND scan, they are not a second ratchet.
